orders.text:
COMP No.4 of 2012
Hon’ble Sudhanshu Dhulia, J.
Mr. Lalit Belwal, Advocate present for 
the petitioner. 
Heard. 
 This petition was dismissed for non￾prosecution, vide this Court’s order dated 
06.03.2014. 
Learned counsel for the petitioner has 
moved Delay condonation application 
alongwith Restoration application and has 
prayed that delay in filing restoration 
application may be condoned. 
Grounds mentioned in the affidavit are 
bonafide & sufficient to condone the delay in 
filing the restoration application. The Delay 
condonation application is allowed. Delay is 
condoned. 
Heard on the restoration application. 
The restoration application is allowed 
on the ground urged. Order dated 
06.03.2014, passed by this Court, is hereby 
recalled. The petition is restored to its 
original number. 
Issue notice to Official Liquidator. 
List this petition after three weeks in 
daily cause list. 
 (Sudhanshu Dhulia, J.) 
12.09.2014 
 JKJ

orders.judge: Hon'ble Mr. Justice Manoj Kumar Tiwari
orders.text:
Misc. Application No. 12329 of 2015 
Misc. Application No. 11548 of 2017 
In 
COMP No. 4 of 2012
Hon’ble Manoj K. Tiwari, J.
 Mr. Anil Kumar Joshi, Advocate for Official 
Liquidator. 
 Mr. Ashutosh Thakral, Advocate, holding brief 
of Mr. P.K. Chauhan, Advocate for the workmen. 
 Mr. Dinkar Singh & Mr. Rakesh Kumar Joshi, 
Advocates for M/s Asset Reconstruction Company 
(India) Limited/ Applicant in CLMA No. 11548 of 
2017. 
 Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
 The applicant in CLMA No. 11548 of 2017 is a 
Asset Reconstruction Company in whose favour the 
lendor (I.C.I.C.I. Bank Ltd.) has executed an 
assignment agreement dated 29.03.2007. Thus, the 
applicant is a Secured Creditor within the meaning of 
Section 2 (zd) (iii) of the Securitisation and 
Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement 
of Security Interest Act, 2002 (hereinafter referred as 
‘the SARFAESI Act, 2002’). 
 By this application (CLMA No. 11548 of 2017), 
applicant has prayed for issuing a direction to the 
Official Liquidator to hand over possession of the 
secured assets (Schedule of Assets given in 
Annexure-H to the application) of M/s Jalpac India 
Ltd. (Company-in-Liquidation) to him so that 
applicant may sell the same under the provisions of 
the SARFAESI Act, 2002. 
 Learned counsel for the applicant submits that 
District Magistrate, Nainital had passed an order 
under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 in 
favour of the applicant on 19.12.2014, however, 
actual physical possession could not be handed over 
to the applicant in view of the order passed by this 
Court on 13.05.2015. 
 Learned counsel for the applicant further 
submits that considerable time has elapsed since 
passing of the order of winding-up by this Court, but 
the Official Liquidator has failed to take the required 
steps to recover the money by putting the assets of 
the Company-in-Liquidation for sale due to which 
applicant, being the largest secured creditor, is 
suffering enormous financial burden, which includes 
huge security charges from the date of possession of 
the assets by the Official Liquidator.   Per contra, Mr. Anil Kumar Joshi, learned 
counsel for Official Liquidator submits that since the 
applicant has submitted a list of valuer in terms of 
the Court’s order dated 24.10.2017 and the valuers, 
named by the applicant as well as by the Official 
Liquidator, have submitted their reports in sealed 
cover, therefore the applicant cannot claim to sell off 
the property under the SARFAESI Act, 2002. 
 In reply, learned counsel for the applicant 
submits that list of valuer was submitted by the 
applicant in deference to the order of this Court and 
submission of such list will not amount to waiver of 
his right to sell the property under the SARFAESI 
Act, 2002. 
 Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Pegasus 
Assets Reconstruction (P) Ltd. v. Haryana Concast 
Ltd. reported in (2016) 4 SCC 47 has held that 
control of or interference with, by Company Court, 
directly or through Official Liquidator is not 
envisaged for sale of a secured asset of a Company 
under Liquidation by a secured creditor under the 
SARFAESI Act, 2002. Paragraph Nos. 22, 23, 24 & 25 
of the aforesaid judgments are extracted below:- 
“22. In contrast, the SARFAESI Act was enacted in 
2002 to regulate securitisation and reconstruction of 
financial assets and enforcement of security interest 
and for matters connected therewith or incidental 
thereto. Inter alia, one of the main objects of this Act is 
to clothe the banks and financial institutions in India 
with power to take possession of securities and sell 
them. All its significant provisions have been noted in 
detail in Mardia Chemicals in which vires of this Act 
were examined and upheld. 
23. A reading of Sections 9 and 13 of the SARFAESI 
Act leaves no manner of doubt that for enforcement of 
its security interest, a secured creditor has been not 
only vested with powers to do so without the 
intervention of the court or tribunal but detailed 
procedure has also been prescribed to take care of 
various eventualities such as when the borrower 
company is under liquidation for which proviso to sub￾section (9) of Section 13 contains clear mandate 
keeping in view the provisions of Sections 529 and 
529-A of the Companies Act, 1956. Since significant 
amendments were introduced in Section 529 while 
inserting Section 529-A through Amendment Act 35 of 
1985, effective from 24-5-1985 and with the aid of a 
non obstante clause in sub-section (1) of Section 529-A 
workmen’s dues were given preference over other dues 
and made to stand pari passu with dues of the secured 
creditors, in case of apparent conflict, this Court 
through various judgments has upheld the proceedings  under the RDB Act as it happens to be a later Act with 
overriding effect over other laws. The interest of the 
workmen in respect of dues payable to them as per 
Sections 529 and 529-A of the Companies Act has 
been protected by permitting, wherever necessary, 
association of the Official Liquidator with the 
proceedings before the Debts Recovery Tribunal under 
the RDB Act. In our considered judgment, the same 
view is required to be taken in context of the 
SARFAESI Act also, for the additional reason that 
Section 13 requires notice to the borrower at various 
stages which in the case of a company under winding 
up being a borrower would mean requirement of notice 
to the Official Liquidator. The Security Interest 
(Enforcement) Rules, 2002 (for brevity “the Rules”) 
framed under the provisions of the SARFAESI Act also 
require notice upon the borrower or his agent at 
different stages. For sale of immovable secured assets, 
as per Rule 8, the authorised officer can take 
possession by delivering a possession notice to the 
borrower and by affixing possession notice on the outer 
door or at some conspicuous place of the property. 
Before the sale also, the authorised officer is required 
to serve to the borrower a notice of 30 days. Thus, the 
Rules also ensure that the Official Liquidator is in 
knowledge of the proceedings under the SARFAESI Act 
in case the borrower happens to be a company under 
winding up. As a borrower, the Official Liquidator has 
ample opportunity to get the details of the workers’ 
dues as ascertained under the Companies Act, placed 
before the authorised officer and seek proper 
distribution of the amount realised from the sale of 
secured assets in accordance with various provisos 
under sub-section (9) of Section 13 of the SARFAESI 
Act.
24. The above discussion supports the view taken by 
the Delhi High Court that no order is required by the 
Company Judge for association of the Official 
Liquidator in order to protect the interest of workers 
and to realise their dues. Sufficient provisions have 
been made for this purpose under the SARFAESI Act 
and the Rules framed thereunder.
25. In the event, in the capacity of a borrower the 
Official Liquidator is not satisfied with the decisions or 
steps taken by the secured creditor or the authorised 
officer, at appropriate stage it has sufficient 
opportunity to avail the right of appeal under Section 
17 of the SARFAESI Act before the Debts Recovery 
Tribunal. There is a right of further appeal under 
Section 18 before the Appellate Tribunal. On the other 
hand, if the view taken by the Punjab and Haryana 
High Court in Pegasus is accepted, there shall be a 
conflict of rights and interest of the secured creditor 
who have the right and liberty to realise their secured 
interest in accordance with the provisions of the 
SARFAESI Act on one hand, and the statutory rights 
and liability of the Official Liquidator acting under the 
orders of the Company Judge as per provisions of the 
Companies Act, on the other. The appellate fora shall 
also differ, leading to a situation of uncertainty and  conflict between the two Acts. In such a scenario, we 
respectfully agree with the Delhi view and disapprove 
that of the Punjab and Haryana High Court.” 
 Learned counsel for the applicant submits that 
applicant would be required to get the movable 
secured assets valued under Rule 5 and immovable 
property valued under Rule 8(5) of the Security 
Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002. He further 
submits that since Official Liquidator represents 
interest of the workmen in the assets, therefore the 
secured creditor will be duty bound to deposit the 
workmen dues with the Official Liquidator in terms of 
second proviso to sub-Section 9 of Section 13 of the 
SARFAESI Act, 2002. The Official Liquidator, if not 
satisfied with the decision or steps taken by the 
Secured Creditor or Authorized Officer, can avail the 
right of Appeal under Section 17 of the SARFAESI 
Act, 2002 and can also avail the right of further 
Appeal under Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, 
as held by Hon’ble Supreme Court in Pegasus Assets 
Reconstruction (P) Ltd. (supra). 
 Having regard to the aforesaid facts and 
reasons, Official Liquidator shall hand over the 
physical possession of the Secured Assets, as 
described in Annexure-H of the application, to the 
applicant within four weeks to enable the applicant to 
proceed in accordance with the SARFAESI Act, 2002 
and the Rules framed thereunder. 
 Without prejudice to the aforesaid order, Official 
Liquidator is directed to invite claims from all 
workmen as per the Company Court Rules within 
four weeks from today. 
 Miscellaneous applications stand disposed of. 
 (Manoj K. Tiwari, J.) 04.04.2019 Navin

applicant may sell the same under the provisions of 
the SARFAESI Act, 2002. 
 Learned counsel for the applicant submits that 
District Magistrate, Nainital had passed an order 
under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 in 
favour of the applicant on 19.12.2014, however, 
actual physical possession could not be handed over 
to the applicant in view of the order passed by this 
Court on 13.05.2015. 
 Learned counsel for the applicant further 
submits that considerable time has elapsed since 
passing of the order of winding-up by this Court, but 
the Official Liquidator has failed to take the required 
steps to recover the money by putting the assets of 
the Company-in-Liquidation for sale due to which 
applicant, being the largest secured creditor, is 
suffering enormous financial burden, which includes 
huge security charges from the date of possession of 
the assets by the Official Liquidator.   Per contra, Mr. Anil Kumar Joshi, learned 
counsel for Official Liquidator submits that since the 
applicant has submitted a list of valuer in terms of 
the Court’s order dated 24.10.2017 and the valuers, 
named by the applicant as well as by the Official 
Liquidator, have submitted their reports in sealed 
cover, therefore the applicant cannot claim to sell off 
the property under the SARFAESI Act, 2002. 
 In reply, learned counsel for the applicant 
submits that list of valuer was submitted by the 
applicant in deference to the order of this Court and 
submission of such list will not amount to waiver of 
his right to sell the property under the SARFAESI 
Act, 2002. 
 Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Pegasus 
Assets Reconstruction (P) Ltd. v. Haryana Concast 
Ltd. reported in (2016) 4 SCC 47 has held that 
control of or interference with, by Company Court, 
directly or through Official Liquidator is not 
envisaged for sale of a secured asset of a Company 
under Liquidation by a secured creditor under the 
SARFAESI Act, 2002. Paragraph Nos. 22, 23, 24 & 25 
of the aforesaid judgments are extracted below:- 
“22. In contrast, the SARFAESI Act was enacted in 
2002 to regulate securitisation and reconstruction of 
financial assets and enforcement of security interest 
and for matters connected therewith or incidental 
thereto. Inter alia, one of the main objects of this Act is 
to clothe the banks and financial institutions in India 
with power to take possession of securities and sell 
them. All its significant provisions have been noted in 
detail in Mardia Chemicals in which vires of this Act 
were examined and upheld. 
23. A reading of Sections 9 and 13 of the SARFAESI 
Act leaves no manner of doubt that for enforcement of 
its security interest, a secured creditor has been not 
only vested with powers to do so without the 
intervention of the court or tribunal but detailed 
procedure has also been prescribed to take care of 
various eventualities such as when the borrower 
company is under liquidation for which proviso to sub￾section (9) of Section 13 contains clear mandate 
keeping in view the provisions of Sections 529 and 
529-A of the Companies Act, 1956. Since significant 
amendments were introduced in Section 529 while 
inserting Section 529-A through Amendment Act 35 of 
1985, effective from 24-5-1985 and with the aid of a 
non obstante clause in sub-section (1) of Section 529-A 
workmen’s dues were given preference over other dues 
and made to stand pari passu with dues of the secured 
creditors, in case of apparent conflict, this Court 
through various judgments has upheld the proceedings  under the RDB Act as it happens to be a later Act with 
overriding effect over other laws. The interest of the 
workmen in respect of dues payable to them as per 
Sections 529 and 529-A of the Companies Act has 
been protected by permitting, wherever necessary, 
association of the Official Liquidator with the 
proceedings before the Debts Recovery Tribunal under 
the RDB Act. In our considered judgment, the same 
view is required to be taken in context of the 
SARFAESI Act also, for the additional reason that 
Section 13 requires notice to the borrower at various 
stages which in the case of a company under winding 
up being a borrower would mean requirement of notice 
to the Official Liquidator. The Security Interest 
(Enforcement) Rules, 2002 (for brevity “the Rules”) 
framed under the provisions of the SARFAESI Act also 
require notice upon the borrower or his agent at 
different stages. For sale of immovable secured assets, 
as per Rule 8, the authorised officer can take 
possession by delivering a possession notice to the 
borrower and by affixing possession notice on the outer 
door or at some conspicuous place of the property. 
Before the sale also, the authorised officer is required 
to serve to the borrower a notice of 30 days. Thus, the 
Rules also ensure that the Official Liquidator is in 
knowledge of the proceedings under the SARFAESI Act 
in case the borrower happens to be a company under 
winding up. As a borrower, the Official Liquidator has 
ample opportunity to get the details of the workers’ 
dues as ascertained under the Companies Act, placed 
before the authorised officer and seek proper 
distribution of the amount realised from the sale of 
secured assets in accordance with various provisos 
under sub-section (9) of Section 13 of the SARFAESI 
Act.
24. The above discussion supports the view taken by 
the Delhi High Court that no order is required by the 
Company Judge for association of the Official 
Liquidator in order to protect the interest of workers 
and to realise their dues. Sufficient provisions have 
been made for this purpose under the SARFAESI Act 
and the Rules framed thereunder.
25. In the event, in the capacity of a borrower the 
Official Liquidator is not satisfied with the decisions or 
steps taken by the secured creditor or the authorised 
officer, at appropriate stage it has sufficient 
opportunity to avail the right of appeal under Section 
17 of the SARFAESI Act before the Debts Recovery 
Tribunal. There is a right of further appeal under 
Section 18 before the Appellate Tribunal. On the other 
hand, if the view taken by the Punjab and Haryana 
High Court in Pegasus is accepted, there shall be a 
conflict of rights and interest of the secured creditor 
who have the right and liberty to realise their secured 
interest in accordance with the provisions of the 
SARFAESI Act on one hand, and the statutory rights 
and liability of the Official Liquidator acting under the 
orders of the Company Judge as per provisions of the 
Companies Act, on the other. The appellate fora shall 
also differ, leading to a situation of uncertainty and  conflict between the two Acts. In such a scenario, we 
respectfully agree with the Delhi view and disapprove 
that of the Punjab and Haryana High Court.” 
 Learned counsel for the applicant submits that 
applicant would be required to get the movable 
secured assets valued under Rule 5 and immovable 
property valued under Rule 8(5) of the Security 
Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002. He further 
submits that since Official Liquidator represents 
interest of the workmen in the assets, therefore the 
secured creditor will be duty bound to deposit the 
workmen dues with the Official Liquidator in terms of 
second proviso to sub-Section 9 of Section 13 of the 
SARFAESI Act, 2002. The Official Liquidator, if not 
satisfied with the decision or steps taken by the 
Secured Creditor or Authorized Officer, can avail the 
right of Appeal under Section 17 of the SARFAESI 
Act, 2002 and can also avail the right of further 
Appeal under Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, 
as held by Hon’ble Supreme Court in Pegasus Assets 
Reconstruction (P) Ltd. (supra). 
 Having regard to the aforesaid facts and 
reasons, Official Liquidator shall hand over the 
physical possession of the Secured Assets, as 
described in Annexure-H of the application, to the 
applicant within four weeks to enable the applicant to 
proceed in accordance with the SARFAESI Act, 2002 
and the Rules framed thereunder. 
 Without prejudice to the aforesaid order, Official 
Liquidator is directed to invite claims from all 
workmen as per the Company Court Rules within 
four weeks from today. 
 Miscellaneous applications stand disposed of. 
 (Manoj K. Tiwari, J.) 04.04.2019 Navin

In pursuance to the permission granted by the 
Coordinate Bench of this Court, permitting the 
secured creditors represented through Mr. Anil 
Kumar Joshi, to sell the assets under Section 14 of 
the SARFAESI Act, he had been consistently 
directed by the orders passed by the Court on 
19.02.2020, 03.09.2020 and 27.10.2021, to deposit 
the sale proceeds before the Official Liquidator as 
the petitioners’ company of which the ARCIL was 
the secured creditor. 
The sale proceeds have not yet been 
deposited before the Official Liquidator, as a 
consequence thereto settlement of claim of the 
Workman and other creditors are at stake. 
The Official Liquidator has submitted a 
report and had invited the claims as would be 
apparent from Annexure B to the writ petition 
submitted by him. 
Looking to the risk factor, which the 
Workman or the other similar creditors are required 
to be satisfied or met with from the sale proceeds 
received, by M/s Asset Reconstruction Company 
(India) Ltd., hence the assets of the Secured 
Creditor who was permitted to sell the secured 
assets, their property would remain attached by the 
Official Liquidator. They are restrained further to 
deal with their assets by transfer, mortgage in any 
manner, except with the prior permission of this 
Court.  In the meantime, if so advised, the secured 
creditors and the representative of Workman may 
also file their counter affidavit(s) to the report 
submitted by the Official Liquidator.
